passages.happening:
The sons of the prophets tell Elisha that the place where they meet with him is too small. They ask to go to the Jordan, where each can cut a log to build a new place, and they ask him to come with them. “I will come,” he replies (verse 3).

As one of them is cutting down a tree, the iron axe head flies off into the water. “Oh, my master,” he cries, “it was borrowed!” (verse 5). Elisha asks where it fell, cuts a stick, throws it in, ‘and made the iron float’ (verse 6). “Lift it out,” he says, and the man reaches out and takes it (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Iron tools were valuable in Israel in this period. A poor member of a prophetic community could not easily replace a borrowed axe head, so losing it meant a debt he could not pay.

The chapter moves from the smallest wonder in the Elisha stories to the largest crisis. This first scene shows the prophet's care for one anxious man and a small loss. God's care stretches from a borrowed tool to the protection of a city.
passages.later: Jesus told his disciples that not one sparrow ‘will fall to the ground apart from the will of your Father’, and ‘you are worth more than many sparrows’ (Matthew 10:29, 31).
passages.asks: The man's panic was over a borrowed tool and a debt he could not pay. Ask what small worry you have not brought to God because it seemed too small. And ask how you treat what you have borrowed from others.

passages.t: Horses and chariots of fire at Dothan
passages.happening:
The king of Aram is at war with Israel. Again and again he plans where to camp, and again and again Elisha warns the king of Israel to avoid that place (verses 8-10). The king of Aram demands to know which of his men is a traitor. A servant answers that ‘Elisha, the prophet in Israel, tells the king of Israel the very words you speak in your bedroom’ (verse 12).

Told that Elisha is at Dothan, the king sends horses, chariots and a great army by night to surround the town (verses 13-14). In the morning Elisha's servant sees them and cries, “Oh, my master, what are we to do?” (verse 15). “Do not be afraid,” Elisha answers, “for those who are with us are more than those who are with them” (verse 16). He prays, “O LORD, please open his eyes that he may see” (verse 17), and the young man sees ‘that the hills were full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha’ (verse 17).

As the Arameans come down, Elisha prays that the LORD will strike them with blindness, and he does (verse 18). Elisha tells them, “This is not the way, and this is not the city. Follow me, and I will take you to the man you are seeking” (verse 19), and he leads them into Samaria. There he prays for their eyes to be opened, and they find themselves inside Israel's capital (verse 20).

The king of Israel asks, “My father, shall I kill them? Shall I kill them?” (verse 21). “Do not kill them,” Elisha replies. “Set food and water before them, that they may eat and drink and then return to their master” (verse 22). The king prepares a great feast and sends them home. ‘And the Aramean raiders did not come into the land of Israel again’ (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
Dothan lay about ten miles north of Samaria, on the main route from the Jezreel Valley into the hill country. It is the place where Joseph's brothers sold him.

The theme that joins the chapter is sight. The servant cannot see the heavenly army until his eyes are opened. The word, paqach, is used almost only of opening eyes, and it is God's act of giving sight. The rare word for the blindness that strikes the Arameans is used elsewhere only of the men of Sodom at Lot's door, and some think it means confusion or dazzling rather than total loss of sight, since the soldiers follow Elisha without knowing him or the road. Either way, God disables the attackers without killing them.

The irony is sharp. The army sent to capture the prophet is captured by him, and the men who came to seize him are led by him. In war captives could be killed or enslaved, and the king's eager question assumes that option. Elisha appeals to a custom of mercy: the king would not kill even men he had taken with his own sword, still less men delivered by God's act. A shared meal created bonds of peace between host and guest. Elisha's prayers are short and specific. They do not change what God is doing so much as ask God to let people see it.
passages.later: A psalm says, ‘The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear Him, and he delivers them’ (Psalm 34:7). Proverbs says, ‘If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat’ (Proverbs 25:21), and Paul quotes the same proverb to the church in Rome (Romans 12:20). Jesus taught, “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you” (Luke 6:27).
passages.asks: The servant saw only the enemy until his eyes were opened. Ask what in your life might look different if you could see what God sees. And ask what it would look like to set a meal before someone who has opposed you.

passages.happening:
Some time later Ben-hadad king of Aram brings his whole army and besieges Samaria. The famine grows so great that a donkey's head sells for eighty shekels of silver (verse 25).

As the king of Israel walks on the wall, a woman cries out, “Help me, my lord the king!” (verse 26). He answers that if the LORD does not help her, he has nothing to give (verse 27). She tells him of a pact with another mother, made in the famine, and of a child who died by it (verses 28-29). The text records it in two verses. These notes do not repeat it.

The king tears his clothes, and the people on the wall see the sackcloth he has been wearing under them (verse 30). Then he swears to have Elisha's head that day (verse 31). Elisha, sitting with the elders, knows the king's messenger is coming and tells them to shut the door (verse 32). The king says, “This calamity is from the LORD. Why should I wait for the LORD any longer?” (verse 33).
passages.hearers:
Ben-hadad, son of Hadad, seems to have been a name or throne name used by more than one king of Damascus. Assyrian records from the 850s and 840s BC name the king of Damascus Hadadezer, and scholars debate whether he is the biblical Ben-hadad under another name; the question remains open. The king of Israel is most likely Jehoram, whose reign ended in 841 BC.

Samaria stood on a steep, isolated hill, strongly fortified, so an enemy's best weapon was starvation. A donkey was an unclean animal under the law, and its head held little meat. Sieges could last months or years. Samaria would later hold out three years against Assyria.

The woman's appeal echoes Solomon's judgment between two mothers in 1 Kings 3. Solomon's wisdom brought justice; this king can do nothing. The word for help, yasha, means to save, and the king is right about where help must come from but wrong in his despair. His sackcloth, worn out of sight, was a sign of mourning and penitence, yet he blames the prophet and then the LORD. The last verse is unclear in Hebrew about who speaks, the messenger or the king, but the words are the court's despair.
passages.later: The covenant had warned of siege and famine as the end of a people who abandoned the LORD (Leviticus 26:29; Deuteronomy 28:53-57), and Lamentations grieves the same horror in Jerusalem's fall (Lamentations 4:10).
passages.hard:
Why does the Bible record something so terrible in a besieged city, and why does the king blame God?

The scene is meant to horrify, and the narrator does not soften it, though he tells it briefly. It is there because it is what the covenant had warned would come to a people who abandoned the LORD and were left to their enemies. The Bible does not present it as God's desire. It shows the depth of misery that war and siege bring, and it grieves it again in Lamentations.

It is not a key for reading any people's suffering now. Nothing here gives anyone a warrant to say that a city under siege, a nation at war or a family in famine is getting what it deserves.

The king's response is revealing. He wears sackcloth under his robes, yet he blames the prophet and then the LORD. Some interpreters think he blamed Elisha because the prophet had counseled waiting on the LORD rather than surrender; others think he simply lashed out at God's representative. Either way the chapter shows a man who grieves the results without turning to the LORD. The next chapter shows that the LORD had not abandoned the city even then.

Grief is not a lack of faith. If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The king wore sackcloth and still gave up waiting for the LORD. Ask where you have given up waiting on God while keeping the outward signs of faith. And ask who near you is crying out for help that you cannot give, and whom you might bring them to.
